records.text: Sky News reported that footage from the day the school was struck showed the distinctive tail fins of a Tomahawk missile and said the United States was the only force in the conflict using Tomahawks.
records.speaker: Sky News

appearances.snippet: Filmed in the afternoon on the day the school was struck, the distinctive tail fins of a Tomahawk missile can be clearly seen. ... America is the only force in this conflict that uses Tomahawks.

verification.notes: Sky News's published investigation reports geolocated footage of a Tomahawk near the school, identifies the missile by its distinctive deployed fins, and reports expert conclusions that the United States was the only belligerent known to possess and deploy Tomahawks in the conflict. This verifies what Sky News reported; it does not imply the visible follow-up missile alone proves which particular missile hit the school.

sources.title: New evidence challenges Trump claim about deadly girls school strike
sources.relevance: Sky's Data and Forensics report identifies the visible missile as a Tomahawk and explains why that points to U.S. forces.

sources.relevance: The later investigation says three experts identified Tomahawks by the distinctive fins and that only the U.S. operated them in the war.

records.text: Sky News said the U.S. weapons were precision-guided missiles capable of following a programmed path and using cameras to observe their route in real time.
records.speaker: Sky News

appearances.snippet: These are precision-guided missiles. They follow a programmed path, they have cameras on the front that can watch what they're doing in real time. They're some of the most uh precise weapons that the US has.

verification.notes: The U.S. Navy describes Tomahawk as a precision weapon guided over a mission-tailored route, with in-flight target updates and an onboard camera that can provide imagery to commanders. Those official capabilities substantively support Sky News's description of a programmed path and real-time observation, though the camera's documented purpose is target-area and battle-damage imagery rather than continuous public video of the entire route.

sources.title: Tomahawk | Naval Air Systems Command
sources.relevance: Official Navy description of the missile's precision guidance, mission-tailored route, two-way communications, in-flight updates, and onboard camera.

sources.title: OPNAV M-8000.16 Volume II
sources.relevance: Official Navy manual describes in-flight communications and the ability to provide a single-frame image along the flight path.

records.text: Sky News reported that a U.S. carrier strike group centered on the USS Abraham Lincoln was within Tomahawk range of Minab on the day of the attack.
records.speaker: Sky News

appearances.snippet: We know that Tomahawk missiles are typically fired from ships and submarines, and we know that on the day of the attack, America had a carrier strike group in the area. This is, I'll get up for you, a satellite image of their carrier strike group with the USS Abraham Lincoln and ... an aircraft carrier and then three warships around it in the Arabian Sea three days before the attack. We have another image which we've been able to use to place them on the day of the attack, based on the information shown on this monitor here, and that puts the carrier strike group right within range of Minab.

verification.notes: Sky News reports that open-source evidence placed the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, including three Tomahawk-capable destroyers, 716 km from Minab on February 28, within the Tomahawk's stated 1,850 km range. This directly confirms the attributed Sky News report.

sources.title: Sky News Minab investigation - U.S. carrier strike group within range
sources.relevance: Reports the strike group's open-source location and the calculated 716 km distance from Minab.
